steps.title: Key Context
steps.body: Poverty was one of the most serious problems in Elizabethan England. The population grew from approximately 3 million in 1550 to over 4 million by 1600, but the economy could not provide enough work or food for everyone. The dissolution of the monasteries (1536-41) had destroyed the main system of charitable support for the poor, and economic changes left increasing numbers of people destitute. The government was forced to create new legislation to deal with the crisis.

steps.title: The Key Distinction
steps.body: Elizabethan people divided the poor into two categories: The "deserving poor": Those who were poor through no fault of their own - the old, the sick, the disabled, widows, orphans, and those temporarily unemployed due to harvest failure. These people deserved sympathy and help. The "undeserving poor": Those who were believed to be poor through their own fault - the idle, the lazy, drunkards, and vagrants who chose not to work. These people deserved punishment, not help. This distinction was central to all Elizabethan poor law legislation.

steps.title: The Harshness of the 1572 Act
steps.body: The 1572 Act was deliberately brutal because it treated vagrancy as a criminal problem, not a social one. Burning through the ear permanently marked a person as a vagrant, making it impossible for them to escape the stigma. The threat of execution for a third offence was extreme, though it was rarely carried out in practice. The Act reflected the fear and anger that vagrants inspired in the propertied classes.

steps.title: How Effective Were the Punishments?
steps.body: The harsh punishments for vagrants were largely ineffective. Whipping and branding did not solve the underlying causes of poverty - vagrants returned to wandering because they had no alternative. The punishments were also difficult to enforce consistently: JPs were often reluctant to carry out extreme sentences; local communities sometimes sympathised with local vagrants; and the system of returning vagrants to their home parish was impractical. The fundamental problem was that legislation treated poverty as a moral failing rather than an economic problem.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always use specific dates: 1572 Vagabond Act, 1576 Poor Relief Act, 1597 Act, 1601 Poor Law Know the distinction between deserving and undeserving poor - it's fundamental to all poor law questions For cause questions, explain EACH cause separately with specific details When discussing legislation, explain both the provisions AND their significance For "how far do you agree" questions, present both sides before reaching a judgement Link the poor laws to the broader context: dissolution of monasteries, population growth, inflation Remember that the 1601 Poor Law lasted 230+ years - this shows its importance
